entities.summary:
Hubert Miles Gladwyn Jebb, 1st Baron Gladwyn, was a pivotal figure in 20th-century British diplomacy and international institutional development, most notably serving as the acting Secretary-General of the United Nations from October 1945 to February 1946. Born on April 25, 1900, Jebb's career spanned the critical transition from the interwar League of Nations era to the Cold War and the establishment of the post-World War II global order. His early tenure at the UN, a nascent organization formed amidst the devastation of war and the dawn of the atomic age, positioned him at the very genesis of modern multilateral diplomacy, shaping its foundational administrative and procedural norms.

Jebb's extensive diplomatic career began in 1929, following his education at Eton College and Magdalen College, Oxford. He served in the Foreign Office, gaining experience in various departments, including the League of Nations section, which provided invaluable insight into the challenges of international cooperation. During World War II, Jebb held key positions, including Head of the Economic Warfare Department and later as a senior official in the Foreign Office, contributing to Allied planning for the post-war world. His experience culminated in his appointment as Executive Secretary of the Preparatory Commission of the United Nations, leading directly to his temporary leadership of the organization as it found its feet in London before establishing its permanent home in New York.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Gladwyn Jebb's role as the acting Secretary-General during the United Nations' critical formative months directly shaped its initial administrative and operational structures. His subsequent career in diplomacy and politics significantly influenced British foreign policy, particularly regarding European integration and Anglo-French relations in the post-war era.
